lossTaxonomy.label: Type 1 — Extinct
lossTaxonomy.definition: No current practitioners; knowledge exists only in historical literature. The original methodological community has dissolved.

lossTaxonomy.label: Type 2 — Vestigial
lossTaxonomy.definition: Practiced in reduced or distorted form; the original intent and theoretical grounding have been lost, leaving only a surface procedure.

lossTaxonomy.label: Type 3 — Siloed
lossTaxonomy.definition: Active in academic or specialist contexts; absent from industry practice. The knowledge exists but does not circulate.

lossTaxonomy.label: Type 4 — Renamed
lossTaxonomy.definition: Rebranded under new terminology; origins unacknowledged. The method continues under a different name without credit or theoretical connection to its origins.
examples: Time-and-motion and task analysis surviving as 'task flows' and journey maps
Critical incident analysis absorbed into thematic coding

lossTaxonomy.label: Type 5 — Latent
lossTaxonomy.definition: Known but rarely used; infrastructure for revival exists. The method is in memory but not in practice.

lossTaxonomy.label: Unmigrated (extended edition)
lossTaxonomy.definition: Not lost in the strict sense: rigorous tools that exist in neighbouring fields and that UX practice could use today but never adopted in the first place.

causesOfDeath.name: Complexity Exceeds Organisational Patience
causesOfDeath.explanation: Powerful methods need training, time, coordination and sustained effort; when pressure intensifies they are the first to be simplified or abandoned. Contextual inquiry was not abandoned because it failed but because it demanded too much.

causesOfDeath.name: Technological Displacement
causesOfDeath.explanation: New interaction paradigms make some methods obsolete or require adaptation (desktop to mobile, software to embedded). A legitimate cause of evolution that often produces death where adaptation would be more appropriate.

causesOfDeath.name: Paradigm Shift in the Field
causesOfDeath.explanation: New theoretical frameworks render methods invisible: the 1990s shift from cognitive to social perspectives deprioritised cognitive-model methods; agile marginalised sequential research methods. Valid methods vanish because their framework is no longer fashionable.

causesOfDeath.name: Loss of Training Infrastructure
causesOfDeath.explanation: Methods survive only while practitioners and institutions teach them. When curricula move on, specialist consultancies close or key textbooks go out of print, the method loses its reproductive capacity (GOMS is in every HCI history but almost no programme teaches its application).

causesOfDeath.name: Competitive Displacement by Faster Methods
causesOfDeath.explanation: Simpler, faster methods win in the market for research; the value of richer output is hard to demonstrate while the cost difference is obvious. The selection pressure is systematic and favours speed over validity.

causesOfDeath.name: Failed Replication and Validity Concerns
causesOfDeath.explanation: Some methods decline because replication fails or assumptions are challenged, a legitimate cause. The problem is distinguishing genuine validity failure from implementation failure: hard-to-implement methods give inconsistent results when done badly, which is misread as invalidity.

causesOfDeath.name: Fashion and Novelty Preference
causesOfDeath.explanation: New methods gain cultural cachet independent of value while established ones become unfashionable through familiarity, systematically disadvantaging older methods regardless of utility.

epidemiologyGlossary.definition: The systematic application of epidemiological thinking (concepts, methods and models) to the study of user experience at the population level.
A design feature, pattern or system property that causes measurable harm to user experience; analogue: biological pathogen (virus, bacterium).

A user or population of users susceptible to the effects of a UX pathogen. Susceptibility varies by individual characteristics (literacy, age, familiarity with conventions) and contextual factors; analogue: human host.

The mechanism or channel through which a UX pathogen spreads: design plagiarism, shared component libraries, industry conventions, regulatory structures and market/platform pressure; analogue: transmission vector (mosquito, air, water).

Harm experienced by users as a result of exposure to a UX pathogen, measured as task failure, decision error, wasted time, financial loss, emotional distress or other user-meaningful outcomes; analogue: disease morbidity.
In severe cases, the complete destruction of a user's ability to accomplish a goal, or in high-stakes domains (medical, legal, financial) a contribution to physical harm or death; analogue: death.
The rate of new UX harm events in a population over a defined time period; analogue: disease incidence.
The proportion of a population currently experiencing UX harm, as a point-in-time or period measure; analogue: disease prevalence.

A state of the design ecosystem in which structural factors (standards, regulation, professional norms, user literacy) make it difficult for harmful design patterns to spread and persist; pursued via individual, product-level and ecosystem-level protection.
Design harm caused by an intervention (regulatory, organisational or technical) intended to protect users; the cookie consent epidemic is the canonical example.

UX Disability-Adjusted Interaction: a composite measure combining time cost and quality-of-experience cost of UX failures into a single population-level unit, weighted by interaction importance and failure severity; analogue: DALY.
Framework for quantifying harm from poor UX across populations in time lost, financial harm and quality-of-experience impairment; analogue: Global Burden of Disease (WHO/IHME).

The average number of additional products that adopt a design pattern for each product that first deploys it; a measure of pattern transmissibility. High-R0 harmful patterns (roach motel, confirmshaming, hidden costs) are regulatory priorities.

Susceptible-Infected-Recovered model adapted to UX: products that have not adopted a pattern (susceptible), have adopted it (infected), or adopted then abandoned it under regulatory or reputational pressure (recovered/resistant).
Highly connected nodes (large platforms, design system providers, influential design publications) with disproportionate influence on pattern spread; priority intervention targets.
Patterns exploiting or overwhelming attention, working memory, decision-making under uncertainty or framing susceptibility; most dark patterns.
Organisational structures that systematically prevent users finding what they need (inconsistent navigation, buried information, misleading categorisation); spread via templates, platforms and CMSs.
Interaction conventions creating systematic errors (misleading affordances, uninformative feedback, invisible status); can mutate when copied into unsafe contexts.
Structural features of platforms, organisations or industries that produce poor UX across many products; not localised in any interface element.

Factors determining susceptibility to UX pathogens: digital literacy; cognitive load; emotional state and stress; time pressure and resources; prior experience; age and generational familiarity; language and culture; disability and accessibility needs; socioeconomic factors affecting device and connectivity.
Copying patterns from successful products without understanding the contextual conditions under which they function safely.
Shared UI libraries and design systems (e.g. Bootstrap, Material Design) that transmit good and bad patterns at scale and velocity.
Normalisation of patterns within an industry; harmful conventions acquire 'epidemiological immunity' as users, regulators and competitors accept them.
Technical constraints, monetisation models and requirements of host platforms (app stores, ad specs, payment rules) pushing products toward harmful patterns.
Behavioural analytics instrumented to detect specific UX failure events as a by-product of normal use; analogue: hospital discharge data, lab reporting.
Periodic structured assessment of representative user populations using standard task batteries, exposure measures and harm reports.
Intensive, standardised monitoring of a few high-harm domains (financial services, healthcare, government, employment platforms).
Establish a case definition, describe by person/place/time, develop and test hypotheses about source, implement and evaluate control measures.
Digital design literacy as a vaccine: inoculation materials that let users recognise and resist manipulative patterns without first being harmed, grounded in inoculation theory.
The spread of good design through awards, open design systems, business-value case studies and regulatory floors; interventions should raise good design's R0.
Measures of how UX harm is distributed across demographic groups (age, education, literacy, language, disability).
A systematic approach to UX that (a) was once practised with regularity and rigour, (b) has largely disappeared from contemporary practice, and (c) retains significant potential value if recovered.
A user interface design that tricks users into doing things they did not intend; a primary category of UX pathogen.
